Score Distribution

Item Scores

Q1 Sensor as Encoder

A temperature sensor acts as an encoder: it converts a physical signal into a form that can be recorded digitally.
True ✓
False
Why. An instrument turns an event in the world into a record; a sensor encodes temperature as numbers

Q2 Correlation and Cause

Production volume and defect rate are strongly correlated. This proves that lowering production will lower the defect rate.
True
False ✓
Why. Correlation cannot say what happens under an intervention; a shared cause, such as rushed overtime, can drive both

Q3 Missing Values Before Filling

Some customer records have missing values. The team should fill them all before checking why they are missing.
True
False ✓
Why. Why a value is missing decides how to treat it; missingness itself can carry information

Q4 Schema Alignment vs Entity Matching

Two systems use different customer IDs. Giving their columns the same names is enough to match each customer.
True
False ✓
Why. Same column names align the schema; deciding which records are the same customer is entity matching, a separate step

Q5 Scaling Before Distance

A model measures customer similarity using age and income. Scaling helps stop income’s larger numbers from dominating the distance.
True ✓
False
Why. Distance adds squared differences; income in millions swamps age in tens. Scaling puts both on one footing

Q6 One-Hot and Order

A model must distinguish low, medium and high priority. One-hot encoding tells the model which level is higher.
True
False ✓
Why. One-hot gives each level its own column with no order between them; ordered levels need ordinal encoding

Q7 Selection vs Extraction

A team wants fewer inputs while keeping each variable’s meaning. Feature selection does this by combining variables into new ones.
True
False ✓
Why. Selection keeps a subset of the original variables, so each keeps its meaning; combining them is extraction, such as PCA
Common slip: both reduce inputs, only extraction makes new ones

Q8 Keys Between Tables

A relational database can store each customer’s details once. Orders can refer to that customer using a key.
True ✓
False
Why. Customers live once in their own table; each order carries the customer key, a foreign key
Common slip: copying customer details into every order

Q9 Flexible Documents

Some customer profiles have fields that others do not. A document store can keep these profiles in the same collection.
True ✓
False
Why. A collection does not force one schema; documents with extra fields sit side by side
Common slip: treating a collection like a table with fixed columns

Q10 Results as Inputs

A SQL query’s result can be a table in another query. A MongoDB aggregation stage can pass its documents to the next stage.
True ✓
False
Why. Both compose: a SQL result is a table another query reads; each stage hands documents to the next

Q11 API or Crawling

You need data from two sites: one has an API; the other only has web pages. Which methods fit the first and second sites?
AWeb crawling; API calls
BAPI calls; web crawling ✓
CAPI calls; sensor measurement
DSynthetic data; web crawling
Why. Use the route the source offers: an API returns structured records; pages without an API need crawling

Q12 Typical Value Under Outliers

A few houses have prices far above the rest. Which measure of a typical price is less affected by these extreme values?
AMean
BRange
CStandard deviation
DMedian ✓
Why. The median depends on order, not size: a few huge prices move the mean, not the middle value

Q13 Same Statistics, Different Shapes

Two stores have the same means, variances and correlation for sales and ad spending. Why still compare their scatter plots?
AMatching statistics mean the data have the same shape
BMatching statistics mean the data have the same outliers
CDifferent patterns can produce the same statistics ✓
DA scatter plot cannot show anything beyond the correlation
Why. Anscombe’s quartet: four datasets share mean, variance and correlation yet look completely different

Q14 Smoothing a Noisy Trend

Sensor readings fluctuate rapidly because of noise. You want a smoother trend on a dashboard. Which method fits?
AMoving average ✓
BOne-hot encoding
CkNN imputation
DZ-score standardization
Why. A moving average replaces each point with the mean of its neighbors, damping short-term noise

Q15 Sampling Every Factory

You need a sample that includes every factory. Some factories have far more records than others. What should you do?
ATake the first records in the combined dataset
BSample only from the largest factory
CRandomly sample at least one record from every factory ✓
DRemove unusually large or small values
Why. Group by factory and draw at least one record from each, so no factory is left out

Q16 SELECT-FROM-WHERE

This query builds a product list. What does the list contain?
SELECT name
FROM Product
WHERE category = 'Electronics';
ANames of Electronics products ✓
BAll fields of Electronics products
CNames of all products
DThe number of Electronics products
Why. SELECT picks the name column; WHERE keeps only Electronics rows

Q17 Basic JOIN

Every product has a matching company. This query builds a supplier report. What does it show?
SELECT p.name, c.country
FROM Product p JOIN Company c
  ON p.company_id = c.company_id;
AThe number of products in each country
BEvery possible product–company pair
CEach product and its category
DEach product and the country of its company ✓
Why. ON pairs each product with the company whose ID matches; company_id is unique, so one row per product

Q18 GROUP BY and Average

A dashboard runs this query. What does each result row describe?
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS average_price
FROM Product
GROUP BY category;
AEach product and its price
BOne average price for all products
CEach category and its average product price ✓
DEach company and its average product price
Why. GROUP BY category makes one row per category; AVG(price) is computed inside each group

Q19 Access Pattern to NoSQL Type

A service must (i) find a session by its token and (ii) follow links between friends. Which types fit, in that order?
AGraph; key-value
BKey-value; graph ✓
CDocument; wide-column
DWide-column; document
Why. A token lookup is a get by key: key-value. Following friend links is traversal: graph

Q20 Aggregation Stages

Each sale records a city, product category and amount. You need total Electronics sales in each city. Which steps?
AKeep Electronics; group by category; sum amounts
BKeep Electronics; group by city; count the sales
CGroup all sales by city; sum amounts; sort totals
DKeep Electronics; group by city; sum amounts ✓
Why. Filter first ($match), then group by city ($group), then sum the amounts ($sum)
Common slip: grouping by category gives one total, not one per city
